source: WHO Bureau du Representant au Niger - Profil de la Republique du Niger (country health profile, c. mid-1976; IRIS dated 1977)
processing_notes: Source confirms zero cholera transmission 1975-01-01..1975-11-30. Source states: 'Le Niger est demeuré indemne de choléra depuis 1974 en dépit de la réintroduction de cas bactériologiques à la suite du pèlerinage de 1975 à La Mecque.'. Evidence type: Documented_Absence. Surveillance system status during absence: operational. Explicit WHO country-office statement that Niger remained free of cholera from 1974 to the time of writing (between Apr and Oct 1976). The only exception it names is the reintroduction of bacteriologically confirmed cases after the 1975 Hajj (Dhu al-Hijjah 1395 = December 1975), so this zero row stops at 30 Nov 1975 and the pilgrim importations are recorded as a presence record (Dec 1975-Jan 1976). Corroboration: WER 'Cholera in 1975' (WER 51(18)) Table 1 lists no Niger notification, and Niger is absent from the 1975 WER notifications index. Surveillance: weekly notifiable-disease bulletin functioning (the profile notes collation errors) and laboratory detection of imported cases shows case detection was operating. National level. [AGENT 3 REVISION 2026-10-03] EXTENDED by Agent 3 (2026-10-03): TL 1975-01-01 -> 1974-08-18, so that one row spans the continuous absence. The WHO country office states Niger 'est demeure indemne de cholera depuis 1974' (this source); the 1974 WER cholera index lists Niger only on pp.94, 103, 195, 226, 260, 315, the last (WER 49(37), metadata 147) carrying the notifications of 28.VII-3.VIII and 11-17.VIII.1974 (1 case each), and the notified 1974 series sums to the WHO annual (287 vs 286/75; Agent 1) - so no case after 17 Aug 1974. The Hajj importations of Dec 1975-Jan 1976 remain a presence record. (reason: Agent 3: zero period extended to the end of the 1974 outbreak (continuous absence, one row)) [AGENT 4 REVISION 2026-10-03] Agent 4 corroboration (primary, US Embassy Niamey cable 1975NIAMEY00594, 13 Feb 1975, https://search.wikileaks.org/plusd/cables/1975NIAMEY00594_b.html): Vice President Sani Sido told a US Senate staff delegation on 11 Feb 1975 that the western mobile health team 'had recently been assigned task of inoculating all El Hadj pilgrims returning from Mecca where they had been exposed to cholera and had succeeded in avoiding outbreak of cholera'. The Dec 1974 Hajj had the largest pilgrimage cholera outbreak in recent years, starting among Nigerian pilgrims and exported by returning hajjis (US Embassy Jidda cables 1975JIDDA00006, 1 Jan 1975, and 1975JIDDA00282, 14 Jan 1975). This supports no outbreak in Jan-Feb 1975. DATING CAVEAT: the WHO country profile's 'reintroduction de cas bacteriologiques a la suite du pelerinage de 1975' may refer to these Jan-1975 returns rather than the Dec-1975 Hajj (Saudi Arabia also notified 50 cases in 1976, WER 52(19)), so bacteriologically positive importations (count unknown) may fall inside this row's Jan 1975 window; no count found, row kept. (reason: Agent 4: primary 1975 cable corroboration and dating caveat)

source: FBIS Daily Report: Middle East & Africa, Vol. V No. 130 (FBIS-MEA-84-130), 5 July 1984 - West Africa/Niger: 'Gastroenteritis Epidemic North of Niamey' (Paris AFP in English 1849 GMT 4 Jul 84, quoting the Niger Health Ministry)
processing_notes: Source states: 'Niamey, July 4 (AFP) - An epidemic of gastro-enteritis has killed 143 people since the end of May along the valley of the Niger River upstream of Niamey, the Health Ministry said today in the Niger capital. The disease, which attacks the linings of the stomach and the intestines, was in some cases complicated by cholera, the ministry said. The epidemic, which has so far affected some 1,700 people in all, was caused by the polluted water of the river ... It has struck villages along a 100-kilometer ... stretch of the river, beginning at a point some 30 kilometers ... from Niamey. However, no cases of the disease have so far been reported in the capital. ... some 50 per day ... The last major cholera epidemic in the arid west African state occured in 1971' - interpreted as 1700 sCh cases, 143 deaths. Interpreted as 1,700 suspected cholera cases (sCh) and 143 deaths, CUMULATIVE since the end of May 1984 to 4 Jul 1984 (TL set to 23 May 1984, the date WHO received Niger's first report of the 1984 cholera outbreak, WER 60(20); onset may be slightly earlier). 'Affected ... people' here means people who fell ill (paired with deaths and '50 [cases] per day'), not an exposed population. The Ministry's public label was 'gastro-enteritis ... in some cases complicated by cholera'; this is the first wave of Niger's 1984 cholera epidemic: WHO first report 23 May 1984; WER 59(28) lists Niamey Departement as the only newly infected area (telegram 9 Jul 1984, 13 cases); Radio Ouagadougou via Monrovia Domestic Service 3 Jul 1984 reports cholera 'in 30 areas of Niger just across the border' with Upper Volta (JPRS-TEP-84-020). LOCATION: villages along the Niger river 30-130 km upstream (north-west) of Niamey, capital explicitly unaffected = today's Tillaberi region (pre-1992 Niamey departement outside the capital). Provincial subset - do not sum with national row (JHU/WHO 1984 annual national 3,788/308); at 4 Jul 1984 this was effectively the whole national count (single focus). Overlaps in time and pre-1992 geography with AI rows 36-38 (IHR notifications for 'Niamey Departement', 23 May-22 Jul 1984, 13+5+1 cases) - do not sum with them; the IHR telegrams reported only a small fraction (bacteriologically confirmed?) of the Ministry's count. CORROBORATION: single source for the count (AFP quoting MoH); outbreak, timing and place corroborated by WHO/IHR and Radio Ouagadougou; magnitude bounded by WHO annual 3,788/308 (1,700/143 = 45%/46% by early July; CFR 8.4% vs annual 8.1%). Confidence 0.45 (Level 3 press source + label ambiguity + single-source count). FBIS-MEA-84-130, West Africa section, Niger. Agent 4.
